title: Tech Talk: 32in is coming to gravel whether we like it or not

Tech Talk: 32in is coming to gravel whether we like it or not

Thanks to more than ten years testing products for Cyclist, tech editor Sam has plenty to say when it comes to new bikes and gear. Tech Talk is Sam’s fortnightly newsletter, with a focus that hops between his thoughts on the latest kit to be featured by Cyclist and wider tech trends that people are talking about, or should be talking about. Click here to get Tech Talk directly to your inbox.

Depending on where you chart it from, the roots of the modern bicycle stretch back nearly 150 years. Taken holistically the basic premise hasn’t really changed to this day, but delving into the minutae of bike design – as tech nerds like me spend our contracted hours (and plenty of extra-curricular time) doing – things have changed pretty drastically. What’s more they don’t even look like slowing down – if anything, the rate of change is increasing.

Take just the past 15 years, for example. The number of sprockets on a cassette has continued to grow, mechanical gearing went to electronic which went to wireless, cable-actuated rim brakes changes to hydraulic discs, tyre widths have nearly doubled on the road… and now we must brace ourselves for what is shaping up to be the most disruptive innovation of the lot: the adoption of 32in wheels.

Modern gravel bikes are another innovation to crop up in that decade and a half, and recently it has looked like they’ve been maturing into a recognisable formula. But in the past few months change has been afoot: spurred on by prototypes in the mountain bike scene, 32in one-offs have been cropping up.

As is so often the case, independent metal builders have been the pioneers, but an increasing number of bigger brands rolling out prototypes in carbon composite is proving that this is a trend shift that will become mainstream.

Gravel bikes even foreshadowed this, flirting as they did with 650b before favouring 700c, citing better stability, comfort and rollover. We should have known things wouldn’t stop there.

Scott provided gravel pro Cameron Jones with a 32in Addict Gravel RC for Unbound earlier in the year, then things quietened down, but the rumours and sightings have picked up again in frequency through the summer.

Harry Tanfield was spotted pootling around at the National Gravel Championships on a Ribble prototype (he raced a on standard Ultra-Grit), Canyon made a song and dance about make a ‘one-off’ 32in Grizl for NBA superstar LeBron James, and there have even been whispers about a bigger brother to Specialized’s new Crux… yep, big brand 32in gravel bikes are on their way.

For what it’s worth, I’m not a particular fan of this development – it smacks of change for change’s sake, and while there’s plenty of that going on already, when the change is this disruptive it’s hard to not view it as more hassle than it’s worth.

That said, it keeps things fresh, and though I don’t want to admit it, will likely only make bikes better to ride (albeit just marginally and without factoring in the logistical nightmare new hub spacing, rim and tyre sizing will introduce to every aspect of the bike industry).

At least it’ll keep me well stocked with new things to write about, so don’t expect these newsletters to dry up any time soon…

The rumour mill

Tech tip-offs from your man in the know

I feel like I’ve dropped some 32in-sized bombs in the column above, so I’ll follow up with a little firecracker here. Some new Shimano S-Phyre shoes are appearing on more and more pros’ feet, suggesting a launch is imminent. Could this be when Shimano chooses to debut the updated pedal and cleat system that undid Matheiu van der Poel race at this year’s Paris-Roubaix, when he couldn’t switch clip in to the current pedals on Jasper Phillipsen’s bike? I wouldn’t bet against it.

Tech tidbits

A couple of small product launch highlights from the past week or two

Super-speedy Continental gravel tyres

Because the size of gravel tyres continues to rise, when it comes to traction width is increasingly being used as a proxy for tread. As such, tread patterns are becoming more minimal and off-road tyres are getting faster. Continental’s new Terra Competitions are a great example: they’re said to be the brand’s fastest ever gravel tyre.

‘Their sleek chevron tread makes them 17% faster than our previous race tyre, the Terra Speed,’ says Continental’s gravel product manager, Alexander Haenke. ‘They’re now fast enough that riders don’t have to choose between road speed and off-road capability.’

The Terra Competitions will be offered in two casings – burlier ‘trail’ and more supple ‘race’ – and three widths 35mm, 40mm and 45mm.

Top-tier Giro shoes with extra protection

The Imperial shoe has been at the top of Giro’s footwear line up since it launched in 2019 and has had one significant makeover in that time. The update didn’t change its proposition though – a highly ventilated shoe for racers in peak racing weather. The WorldTour season is long, mind you, and the amateurs that want pro-level performance in their shoes will be riding whatever the weather too. With that in mind, Giro has created an ‘All Season’ branch on the Imperial tree.

‘Given the Imperial is such a common shoe in the WorldTour peloton, we’re able to get plenty of feedback from the pros that use them,’ says Raphaël Dalle, Giro’s footwear development director. ‘Riders such as Jay Vine and Thymen Arensmen love the Imperial for their light weight and ventilation but find them hard to clean. We thought by reducing the exposed mesh areas in the All-Season and increasing the coverage of the TPU film bonded over the top, we could kill two birds with one stone. This improves protection and insulation against grotty weather and makes them easier to keep clean.’

Despite the reconfigured upper, Dalle says the shape and carbon outsole are the same as the Imperial II, so existing users should be able to swap between them seamlessly. The weight remains within a few grams (243g vs 235g) as well, so the Imperial AS shoes look to provide the same performance, just with a little extra practicality.
